issues.legal_issue: A notification describing the resettlement of immigrants serves the statutory purpose of settling immigrants.
material_facts: The acquisition notification stated that the land was needed for the resettlement of immigrants who had migrated because of circumstances beyond their control.
The governing statute described the relevant public purpose as the settlement of immigrants.
issues.conclusion: In this context, “settlement” and “resettlement” express the same purpose: providing habitation and other amenities to displaced immigrants.
issues.legal_principle: Section 2(d)(i) of the West Bengal Land Development and Planning Act, 1948 makes the settlement of qualifying immigrants a public purpose. The Court interpreted that provision by its intent and held that using “resettlement” in the notification rather than “settlement” did not take the acquisition outside that purpose. No earlier cases were relied on for this issue.

predicates.land_acquisition_challenge: A party challenges an acquisition of land for a stated public purpose.
predicates.notice_identifies_migrant_resettlement: The acquisition notice states that the land is needed to resettle immigrants displaced by circumstances beyond their control.

issues.definition: When a land-acquisition challenge concerns a notice identifying migrant resettlement as its purpose, that purpose counts as statutory settlement.

issues.legal_issue: A hospital serving displaced people can form part of their settlement and rehabilitation, so its later identification as a use for acquired land does not by itself show that the acquisition had a different purpose from the one notified.
material_facts: The notification stated that the land was needed for the resettlement of immigrants who had migrated because of circumstances beyond their control.
Later departmental correspondence recorded that the land was to be made available for a hospital for crippled children.
The correspondence connected the hospital proposal to refugee relief and rehabilitation, and other correspondence described medical facilities as being developed in the interest of displaced persons.
The respondents relied on the later correspondence to contend that the actual purpose differed from the notified purpose and that the acquisition was in bad faith.
issues.conclusion: Providing a hospital, including one for crippled children of displaced people, falls within their rehabilitation and settlement. The later correspondence did not establish a different purpose that invalidated the notification.
issues.legal_principle: Section 2(d)(i) of the West Bengal Land Development and Planning Act, 1948 treats settlement of qualifying immigrants as a public purpose. Rehabilitation includes providing shelter, food, medical care, and other necessary amenities; a hospital serving displaced people can therefore be part of settlement. Section 8(1)(b) of that Act applies the compensation framework of section 23 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, subject to the stated restriction for acquisitions for the purpose in section 2(d)(i). The Court held that subsequent internal correspondence about a rehabilitation amenity did not establish that the notified purpose was different. No earlier cases were relied on.

rule.if: land_acquisition_challenge and notice_identifies_migrant_resettlement and later_records_describe_hospital_plan and hospital_serves_displaced_people

predicates.land_acquisition_challenge: A party challenges an acquisition of land for a stated public purpose.
predicates.notice_identifies_migrant_resettlement: The acquisition notice states that the land is needed to resettle immigrants displaced by circumstances beyond their control.
predicates.later_records_describe_hospital_plan: Records created after the acquisition notice describe a plan to use the land for a hospital.
predicates.hospital_serves_displaced_people: The planned hospital is intended to provide medical care to displaced people or their children.

issues.definition: If a challenged acquisition is notified for migrant resettlement and later records describe a hospital intended to serve displaced people, the acquisition serves a qualifying public purpose.

issues.legal_issue: Unexplained substantial delay in bringing a writ challenge to an acquisition may justify withholding discretionary writ relief.
material_facts: The notification and subsequent declaration preceded the writ petition by more than two years and two months.
The Single Judge found that the respondents had given no satisfactory explanation for the delay and declined to exercise the discretionary jurisdiction under Article 226.
The Supreme Court allowed the appeal and restored the Single Judge’s judgment after the Division Bench had reversed it on delay and merits.
issues.conclusion: The Single Judge’s refusal to exercise discretionary writ jurisdiction because of the unexplained delay was restored.
issues.legal_principle: The Court restored the Single Judge’s conclusion that discretionary relief under Article 226 should not be exercised where the challenge was brought after substantial delay without a satisfactory explanation. The judgment cites no earlier cases for this issue.

predicates.writ_challenge_to_land_acquisition: A claimant seeks writ relief challenging a land-acquisition proceeding.
predicates.challenge_brought_after_substantial_dela: The claimant brings the challenge a substantial time after the relevant acquisition steps.
predicates.delay_unexplained: The claimant provides no satisfactory explanation for the delay.

issues.definition: When a claimant brings a land-acquisition writ challenge after substantial delay and does not satisfactorily explain it, discretionary writ relief is denied.
